Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00349

The first is what is necessary in itself: the First Reality, the Light of lights, as the Illuminationists call it; true unity, in the language of the Pythagoreans; and the Reality of realities, in the language of the mystics. The second cannot be impossible in itself, since we began by considering something that exists. Let us call it possible, whether it is an essence or a mode of existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00350

An essence is existent when existence is joined to it and gives it its color. A mode of existence is existent because it proceeds from a complete maker, like light and shadow falling on forms that receive them. More precisely, modes of existence take on different forms: they are described through essences as colored by them, joined to them, or brought to greater completeness; and they are described in relation to the One who sustains them as dependent, descending, shining, appearing, or flowing forth—language suited to His transcendence and self-sufficiency.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00351

When we say that something “exists” and draw the general idea of an existent from it, the basis for that claim, in what is necessary in itself, is simply its own reality. We do not have to consider anything added to it, or any feature that explains or qualifies it. In what is possible, by contrast, the basis for saying that it exists is something else: a feature joined to its essence if we mean an essence, or a relation of dependence if we mean a mode of existence. Proof will show that the existence of what is possible comes only through its union with the reality of existence. Its possibility lies in depending on something else. What is necessary is existence that depends on nothing else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00352

So when we speak of the possibility of essences outside the concept of existence, we mean that, considered in their own nature, they are neither necessarily existent nor necessarily nonexistent. The possibility of modes of existence, by contrast, means that they are inherently related to and dependent on something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00353

Universal essences may not be real before existence, but as long as they exist—even in the mind—they can be understood in their full nature. Before they are lit by the light of existence, however, they cannot be pointed out in thought as either existent or nonexistent. They remain hidden in themselves, veiled in their original concealment, forever. We can refer to them and say that they are what they are, and nothing but what they are: neither existent nor nonexistent, neither earlier nor later, neither source nor result, neither dependent nor maker nor made. In themselves, even when they exist, we do not describe them by any feature other than what they are. Mystics sometimes speak of essences as though they had such features, but they do so figuratively.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00354

Existence modes are different. Their very reality is dependence. The mind cannot point to them as independent things, as though they were separate from the One who sustains them. They have no independent identity. Yet they are entirely real: actual existences without ambiguity, clear existence without an underlying essence, pure light without darkness. This is a level beyond ordinary thought, because understanding it requires an unusually clear and subtle mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00355

A composite essence cannot be fully understood through its definition until we understand the parts that make it what it is. In the same way, we cannot fully understand any dependent mode of existence until we understand what makes it exist: its principles and the causes that bring it about. Those who look deeply at what logicians say about proof and definition will find a subtle sign of this. A proof and a definition can share the same central element: the middle term in a proof—the cause introduced by “because”—is the very feature that completes a definition. It is what makes a thing what it is. Aristotle makes a similar point in Theology: for many things, the answer to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” is one and the same.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00356

In short, only the mind can separate a possible thing from what makes it real, whether we are speaking of its essence or its existence. We have seen why: whatever is possible in itself and dependent by nature cannot bring about its own existence, either wholly or in part. Nor can it make existence more likely than nonexistence, or the reverse, whether or not either side reaches necessity. To suppose that a possible thing, in itself, could favor existence before it exists is to forget that, apart from its cause, it is sheer nothing. It has no distinction, power, or tendency of its own.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00357

There is another reason a possible thing cannot make its own existence more likely. Before it exists, it has no distinctness or particular form. Suppose one possible thing gave itself a greater claim to a certain form of existence, while another did not. Before either exists, nothing distinguishes them at that level. One would therefore be favored without a reason, and given a particular form without anything to determine it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00358

The idea of possibility that applies to all possible things is expressed in God's words: “Everything will perish except His Face.” To perish is to have no claim to existence. God excepts His Face: the aspect of necessity, which is existence in its full actuality. This sacred meaning is also heard in the words of Labīd: “Everything apart from God is empty and false, and every delight must pass away.” The Prophet's soul was stirred by this in a high, holy way, not by a bodily pleasure. He rejoiced and said: “O God, the true life is the life of the Hereafter.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00359

The word “real” has several meanings. It can mean actual existence in general; lasting existence; or what is necessary in itself. It can also describe a statement or belief that matches what exists outside the mind: we say that a statement is true, or a belief is true. In this last sense, “truth” means that a statement matches reality. Some people wrongly think the difference is that “real” means reality matches the statement or belief, while “true” means the statement or belief matches reality. This distinction is strained.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00360

The strongest truths are statements that remain true at all times. More basic still are principles that are true in themselves. First among them is this: between affirming something and denying it, there is no third possibility. Every statement rests on this principle when we trace it back to its foundations. Reject it, and every premise and conclusion falls with it. This truth belongs to anything that exists, simply insofar as it exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00361

Avicenna offers a clear way to answer the sophists in The Healing. Ask them: “Do you know that your denial is true or false, or do you doubt it?” If they say they know one of these, they admit that at least one belief is true, whether it is the belief that their denial is true, that it is false, or that it is doubtful. Their denial of truth in general then fails.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00362

If they answer that they doubt, ask them: “Do you know you are doubting? Do you know you are denying things? Do you know any particular statement?” If they acknowledge even one of these things, they have admitted that some knowledge and some truth are possible. If they say they understand nothing—not even that they understand nothing—and doubt everything, including their own existence and nonexistence, their doubt about their doubt, and their denial of everything, including their denial, there is no point in arguing with them or hope of guiding them. Their only remedy is to make them enter a fire, if they claim that fire and no fire are the same, or to strike them, if they claim that pain and no pain are the same.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00363

The division of ideas into what is necessary, possible, and impossible is a real division, or at least one that serves the same purpose. Once our minds are working properly, we can set aside the idea that both sides of existence and nonexistence—or affirmation and denial—could each be necessary. The same division applies to every concept in relation to any predicate: a concept may necessarily be an animal, necessarily not an animal, or possibly an animal. But in general metaphysics, the words “necessary,” “possible,” and “impossible” immediately bring to mind what is necessary, possible, or impossible in relation to existence. This is the same division used in logic, but there it is restricted to one particular predicate: existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00364

Some people object that necessity must mean something different when we speak of a feature belonging to an essence. Otherwise, they say, every feature that necessarily follows from an essence would itself exist necessarily. The answer is simple: four must be even, but four need not exist of itself. What changes is what we are saying about the subject, not the meaning of necessity.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00365

Some writers raised this objection because they did not understand the issue. A feature that necessarily follows from an essence—such as evenness following from the number four—is attributed directly to the essence itself. For possible things, it depends on a maker only indirectly, because such things do not become actual except through creation. It also depends on existence only indirectly: the feature belongs to the essence when the essence is actual, not because the cause that makes it actual must be made up of the essence plus an added existence, or because the statement is conditional on the essence's existence. Yet some thinkers confused these cases. They assumed that a feature such as evenness is necessary only on the condition that the essence exists. They did not distinguish this from a necessity that is conditional on a description or feature.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00366

They also failed to distinguish this kind of necessity from what is necessary in itself for all eternity, as when we say that God is necessarily powerful and wise. Three cases must be kept apart: what is necessary for a time, what is necessary for as long as a thing exists, and what is necessary in itself forever. Remember the difference. It helps us see how a feature can belong necessarily to an essence while that essence exists, without depending on its existence as the reason for the feature.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00367

This kind of necessity—true of something while it exists, but not caused by its existence—is shared by the essential features that come first and the properties that follow from them. What differs is their order in relation to the essence: one belongs to its nature first, the other follows from it. That order is a priority of nature, not a familiar kind of causal priority.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00368
Chapter — Necessary existence cannot depend on another; no necessary link joins two necessary beings
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00369

If we suppose two beings necessary in themselves, neither can also be necessary through a cause. As you have learned, something is necessary in itself when, considered entirely on its own, it is correct to say of it that it exists and is existent, without adding any other feature—whether the feature is joined to it, abstracted from it, used to limit it, or used to explain why the statement applies.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00370

Sometimes a statement applies to the subject without any further condition or cause. This is eternal necessity in itself. Sometimes it applies to the subject without an added condition or cause, but only while the subject is as it is. This is called essential necessity: “A human being is an animal,” or “A human being is a human being.” Sometimes a statement applies because of a reason beyond the subject itself. In other cases, we consider the subject together with an added condition. That condition may be negative (“Zayd is blind”), relational (“The sky is above us”), a matter of thought (“Zayd is possible”), or something joined to the subject (“Zayd is white”).
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00371

The existence of what is necessary in itself is a case of eternal necessity. The idea “existent” applies to it when we consider its own reality alone, without adding any other meaning or feature. Now suppose that such a reality depends on an outside cause. Would it still exist if that cause were removed, supposed absent, or set aside in our reasoning? If it would, the cause makes no difference to its existence. But we supposed that the cause produced it—a contradiction. If it would not exist without the cause, then it was never necessary in itself. Both possibilities are impossible, so the original assumption is false: what is necessary in itself cannot also be necessary through another. Anything necessary through another is possible in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00372

It also follows that there cannot be a necessary relation between two things that are each necessary in themselves. A relation of necessity holds only between things where one is the cause of the other, or where both depend on one cause, directly or through an intermediary. When things have no causal relation, dependence, or connection, the mind can suppose that one exists without the other. So if two necessary beings were necessarily linked, one of them—or both—would have to depend on the other. It would then be possible rather than necessary in itself, which is a contradiction.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00373

Here is another way to see it. If two necessary beings were necessarily connected, two existences would have to come together in a single reality: one existence through itself, because it is necessary, and another through the other being, because of their necessary connection. The connection itself is clear enough; what it implies is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00374

What is necessary, considered simply as necessary, does not become necessary in relation to something it does not need, whether that other thing is necessary or possible. Nor does necessity in itself rule out a thing's being possible in relation to something else, or the other thing being possible in relation to it. This is ruled out only if they stand in a relation of cause and effect, or in a necessary connection of dependence. As we have seen, no such relation can hold between two beings that are necessary in themselves.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00375

So if we suppose two beings necessary in themselves, they cannot be linked by their very natures. At most, they would happen to exist alongside each other. In relation to the other, each would still be possible. Two related things whose existence depends on their being together cannot be established by their own realities alone; the relation requires a third thing that gives rise to it. This is explained in the discussion of proof, where the author shows how each of the two is defined and why the definition must include the cause that establishes their relation, rather than the other related thing itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00376
Chapter — The Necessary Being has no essence apart from His existence
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00377

This means that God has no essence distinct from His own pure existence. A possible thing, such as a human being, has an essence—rational animal—and an existence, the fact that it is real outside the mind. There are several reasons to show that this is not true of God.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00378

First, suppose God's existence were not identical with His reality. Although He is simple, as we will show, He would then both receive existence and produce it. Why? If existence were added to His essence, its cause would have to be either that essence, as the subject of the feature, or something else. If something else caused it, God would depend on another and would be possible rather than necessary. So His essence would have to receive existence as its subject and produce existence as its cause. There is a problem with this conclusion that we will return to, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00379

Second, if existence were added to God's essence, the thing would have to exist before its own existence—a contradiction that is clear without further argument. The author of The Discussions gives another proof: it would amount to the same thing existing twice and lead to an endless series. But the contradiction is simpler. If existence belonged to essence as an accident belongs to its subject, then existence would depend on essence. It would be possible and would need a cause. If that cause were God's essence, the essence would have to exist before its existence. This is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00380

Third, suppose existence were something added to God’s essence. Then His existence could cease. But that is plainly impossible. Here is why. If existence depends on something other than itself, it is possible in itself and could, considered in itself, cease to be. If it cannot cease to be, it must be necessary in itself, independent of essence. That contradicts our assumption.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00381

But there is a difficulty. Something can be possible in itself and yet necessary because of something else. Suppose we say that the existence added to God’s essence could cease, considered solely in itself. We can grant this. It does not follow that it could cease when considered in relation to the essence that makes it necessary. On this view, the essence itself requires its own existence, and this making-necessary rules out the specific kind of possibility in question. But if the claim is that existence could cease even when we consider the essence that requires it, we reject the claim for the reasons already given.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00382

The main objection raised in The Discussions against the second—and strongest—of our three arguments is this: Why could the essence itself not cause existence, considered simply as an essence, without existing first? The essential parts of an essence come before the whole, not through their existence but through what they are. An essence also causes the features that necessarily follow from it, without first existing. And a thing that receives existence must come before existence, even though it does not yet exist.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00383

Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi answers this in several books, including his commentary on Pointers, The Critique of the Revelation, and The Abstract. The question concerns what causes existence, or something that exists outside the mind. Reason tells us that a cause of existence must come before its effect through its own existence. Until we consider something as existent, we cannot consider it as the source that gives existence. The case of something that receives existence is different. To think of it as receiving existence, we must first consider it without assuming that it already exists; otherwise it would already have what it is to receive. Nor may we assume that it is nonexistent, for that would introduce the opposite difficulty. We therefore consider it simply as an essence, without ascribing existence or nonexistence to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00384

In contrast, the parts that define an essence come before that essence, and the essence comes before its necessary features, only in thought. This is not the same as a body existing before its whiteness.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00385
Avicenna’s The Book of Discussions contains a passage that supports this answer:
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00386

Existence cannot be caused by an essence, because existence has no state other than being existent. The cause of something that exists must itself exist, and the cause of something nonexistent must itself be nonexistent. The cause of a thing insofar as it is a thing, or of an essence insofar as it is an essence, is a thing or an essence. But just because something, considered as an essence, is the cause of some things does not mean it is the cause of everything.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00387

An essence cannot cause existence as one of its necessary features. This has been explained in The Healing and Pointers. In general, anything that causes something actually to exist must itself exist. If an essence caused existence simply because it was an essence, existence would follow from it even while it was nonexistent, because a feature belonging to an essence as such belongs to it however we consider that essence. But an essence cannot cause something to exist before the essence itself exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00388

If the cause does not exist, the effect cannot exist either. At most, the cause may have an essence, and the essence of an effect may follow from it in thought. For example, it follows from the nature of a triangle that its angles equal two right angles. But the equality of those angles does not exist as a fact unless the triangle exists. If no triangle exists, the equality of its angles does not exist either.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00389

Nor can someone say that existence has an essence considered apart from existence, as the equality of a triangle's angles with two right angles has an essence that can be considered without its actual existence. That kind of essence exists when the triangle exists and does not exist when the triangle does not exist. The essence of existence is different: it cannot be nonexistent in any condition. If it is an essence, it must always exist. Nor can anyone say that, considered simply as an essence, it entails only the essence of existence, while, once existence is added, it entails the existence of that essence of existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00390

Someone may object: if the essence of the Necessary Being did not exist, existence would not exist either. So it is not the essence that causes existence, but the essence as an existent thing. Then it must already exist for existence to follow from it; otherwise it would entail only nonexistence. So existence would have to belong to the essence before the essence caused existence. That is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00391
Keep this argument in mind. It has no equal in this discussion.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00392

A criticism and clarification. As you already know, existence is not added to an essence in the way that a feature belongs to the thing bearing it. That would give the essence one existence of its own and then another existence added to it. But existence is the very being of the essence: it is what makes the essence real and definite. Considered by itself, an essence is hidden and obscure. Through existence it becomes real, illuminated, and manifest. Essence and existence are united; one is not attached to the other as a separate thing. Two complete things cannot be united in this way. Unity is possible only between something complete and something incomplete, as between a general kind and its distinguishing feature when considered as such—not when they are treated as mental versions of matter and form.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00393

Only in thought does existence appear to be a feature applied to essence. The mind divides a real thing into a vague essence and the existence that makes it real, then describes the essence as existent. But an essence, precisely because it is vague, cannot cause something definite—least of all the very reality that makes it definite. Without that reality, it has no definite being at all. What makes it definite is its very definiteness, just as something genuinely relative is nothing apart from its relation to what it concerns.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00394

Parts that define an essence may come before the whole they make up. An essence may also come before a feature that necessarily follows from it. But neither is the kind of priority we mean here. We are asking what comes first as a cause. Could essence come before its own existence in that sense? No, for several reasons. We have shown that essence and existence are united in reality, with neither preceding the other. What truly exists is existence; essence is an idea drawn from it and united with it. When scholars say that real existence comes before essence outside the mind, they mean that existence alone is what proceeds from the maker and is established in reality, because existence is that very reality. Essence is a concept drawn from existence and united with it, and so is secondary in this respect—not something caused or changed by existence. Essences are not made, whether by a simple act of creation or by combining parts; we will explain this later.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00395

In short, before the maker brings a possible thing into existence, there is no essence existing there. Once existence comes about, the essence is established with it—not at an earlier or later level. The essence has no independent existence of its own.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00396

There is another reason. Features that necessarily follow from an essence are abstract ideas, not independently real things. We have established that existence is real. How, then, could real existence be a necessary feature of essence? The priority between an essence and its necessary feature can be considered without bringing existence into the discussion only at the level of abstract ideas. But once we consider them as actually existing, neither can be separated from its existence. An essence's power to entail a feature comes together with existence, even though that power does not depend on existence. How, then, could existence itself be a feature that follows from essence, when it is at the very same level and does not come after it?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00397

To clarify: a thing is either an essence or existence. By “essence” here we mean what is not existence: a universal, vague idea. Such an idea can cause one feature, and that feature can cause another. But it cannot cause its own existence, because a cause must come before its effect through its own existence, and what is not existence cannot exist before existence. This also shows that what is necessary in itself cannot be anything other than existence. Anything other than existence cannot cause its own existence; it would then depend on a cause and would not exist through itself. What is necessary in itself, therefore, is existence itself, existing through itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00398

An objection: the same argument seems to apply to existence. If existence causes its own being existent, and a cause has to exist first, then existence would come before its own existence. The answer is that existence is existent through itself, not through some further existence. So we do not mean that existence is existent because it already existed. We mean that existence itself comes before its own being called “existent.” That causes no problem. What is other than existence, by contrast, could come before its own being existent only through existence. It cannot do so through itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00399

Here is another way to see why everything other than existence needs a cause. Take a human being. Does that person exist simply by being human, or through a cause outside humanity? Not simply by being human. A person is human only when that person exists. If being human caused the person to exist, that person would have to exist already in order to exist—which is impossible. The existence of a human being must therefore have an outside cause. The argument also works in reverse: whatever has no cause cannot be something other than existence. It must be existence itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00400

Someone might say that existence itself must also be existent through something else. Otherwise, it could not be existent just because it is existence: it would be existence only if it were existent, and then it would be existent because it was already existent. That leads to the same impossibility. The answer is that existence is existent not through another existence, but through itself. So when we say “existence is existent,” we do not mean that it is existent because it was already existent. We mean that existence is existent through itself. It does not follow that existence must be existent before it is existent. What follows is only that existence comes before its own being called “existent” through itself, and there is no problem in that.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00401

So things other than existence are real through existence, while existence is real through itself. Consider time: things come before or after one another in time, but time needs no second time to establish that order. Bodies are distinguished through matter, while matter is distinguished through itself. Things become visible through light, but light needs no second light to make it visible. This is how some philosophers have explained the matter, though the argument still requires examination.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00402

Fourth, the author of The Book of Flashes offers this argument. If the thing whose existence the mind separates from its essence were impossible by its very essence, none of its instances could exist. But once one instance exists, the universal has other conceivable instances without end. Their essences are not impossible; they are possible. As you have learned, possibility remains even after one instance of a universal has become real.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00403

Now suppose the Necessary Being has an essence apart from existence. Consider that essence on its own, as a general nature. Nothing in it would rule out another individual of the same nature. If the essence made existence impossible, then even the Necessary Being we know exists would be impossible. That is absurd. Perhaps an outside obstacle prevents another individual from existing. But then the essence itself still allows existence; it is possible, not necessary. All its other conceivable individuals would be possible too. The Necessary Being would thus be possible through its own essence. That is a contradiction.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00404

Therefore, if there is a Necessary Being, it cannot have an essence beyond existence—something the mind could separate from existence into two things. It is pure, unqualified existence, untouched by either universality or particularity. That is his argument. May God illumine his spirit. I regard it as a strong proof and a sound explanation.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00405

Someone objects: why can the mind not separate an existing thing into existence and something that receives it, while taking that recipient to be a particular, not a universal? It does no good to restrict the word “essence” to what is universal, since the point is that existence is not an addition to God's reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00406

The answer is that this argument rests on the principle that a thing's being particular is itself a kind of existence. That is the position of those who hold the truth, and al-Farabi states it explicitly. So anything the mind separates into a recipient and existence must, considered in itself and apart from existence, be universal. Anything with a universal essence can have instances other than those that happen to exist, unless something outside the essence prevents them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00407

The argument comes down to this. When we call a thing necessary, possible, or impossible, we are considering what it is in itself in relation to existence. One of these three must apply to any essence considered in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00408

If the supposed Necessary Being were something other than existence, it would have a universal meaning with conceivable instances. Those instances would have to be either all impossible in themselves, all necessary in themselves, or all possible in themselves. Every option fails. The first contradicts the existence of the actual Necessary Being. The second contradicts the fact that the other possible instances have not occurred. The third contradicts the necessity of the instance that does occur. Since all three options fail, the assumption fails: the Necessary Being cannot have an essence beyond existence. If there is a Necessary Being, it is pure, intensified existence, particular through itself, with neither universality nor particularity added to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00409

The objection some scholars raise against this argument is especially weak. They say that it has not been shown that there must be infinitely many possible instances beyond the ones that exist. Why could a universal essence not have a fixed, finite number of instances in reality, even if we can imagine more? And even if there were infinitely many, perhaps that would mean only that their number has no fixed limit; the alleged consequence would not be impossible. Or, if it meant an actual infinity, the most it would show is that there are infinitely many necessary beings. Someone could deny that this is impossible, arguing that proofs against an infinite regress, if valid, would show only that infinitely many ordered things cannot coexist.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00410
But this does not show that necessary beings must form an ordered series; indeed, the opposite is clear.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00411

Our answer begins with the nature of an essence. Considered simply in itself, a general essence fixes neither a finite nor an infinite number of individuals. It fixes no particular degree of individuation at all. If we put aside conditions outside the essence, reason cannot rule out infinitely many individuals of that nature.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00412

The other two objections miss the point as well. We are not trying to disprove an endless number or sequence of necessary beings, whether arranged in order or existing side by side. Some thinkers have questioned whether that is even impossible. Our point is different. If the Necessary Being had a general essence, we could conceive other individuals sharing that essence. The essence, taken by itself, does not determine which of those individuals exists. It does not exclude individuals that never come to exist.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00413

Necessity, possibility, and impossibility belong to a meaning in itself, apart from what happens outside it. Every meaning in itself must be either necessary, possible, or impossible. So if one instance of a universal essence were necessary in itself, all its instances would be necessary in themselves. The same would be true if that instance were impossible or possible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00414

But the other conceivable instances cannot be necessary in themselves, since they have not occurred. They cannot be impossible in themselves either, since then the instance that does occur would also be impossible. Nor can they be possible in themselves, since then the Necessary Being would be possible in itself. We have established that none of these three can be true. Therefore, if God is necessary in Himself, He cannot have an essence other than His existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00415

An objection, and its answer: you may say that philosophers have stated that each separate intellect is particular by virtue of its essence, meaning that the essence of each immaterial substance confines its kind to a single individual. Why should the Necessary Being not have an essence that, by its very nature, is confined to one? How, then, can you say that essence determines no degree of individuation?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00416

Understand that saying the particularity of each intellect belongs to its essence does not mean that universal essence itself demands particularity. We have already indicated that what makes something particular—in the sense of what gives it its particularity—is its own existence. As you have learned, existence is not something essence itself demands.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00417

Here, “belongs to its essence” can mean simply that the two cannot be separated, whether or not one causes the other. That is what philosophers mean when they say that each intellect's particularity belongs to its essence. But particularity can also mean the state of being particular. This is a mental notion, and it can belong to an essence in any sense, because it is not some distinct thing that makes an object particular.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00418

The fifth proof resembles an argument of Suhrawardī and fits Aristotle’s followers’ understanding of substance. If existence were added to the Necessary Being’s essence, His essence would have to belong to the category of substance.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00419

That substance would need a feature defining it, so God’s essence would be made up of parts. That is impossible. There is another difficulty. Whatever is possible for an individual is possible for its nature considered in itself, while whatever is impossible for the nature is impossible for each of its individuals. Some substances are clearly possible: we see material things come into being and pass away. So possibility must belong to substance considered as a general category. If the Necessary Being fell under that category, He would be possible in that respect, not necessary in Himself. That contradicts the supposition.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00420

Anything with an essence beyond existence must therefore be either a substance or an accident. But the Necessary Being is not a substance, as we have shown, and cannot be an accident, since He does not exist in something else. So He has no essence apart from existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00421
Objections and replies
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00422
Several objections have been made to the claim that the Necessary Being is pure existence, with no essence added to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00423

Here is the first. If God’s existence is separate from essence, what accounts for this separation? If it follows from existence itself, then every existence must be separate from essence: what follows from a thing’s nature cannot fail to belong to it. We would then have many Necessary Beings, which is impossible. But if the separation comes from something else, God would depend on that other thing for His necessity. His necessity would depend on the separation, and the separation on something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00424
Someone might say that existence is separate simply because nothing requires it to be joined with an essence. But then it would depend on the absence of whatever would make it joined.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00425

The answer is that God is separate from essence through His own particular existence. For Aristotle’s followers, that existence differs in its very reality from all other existences. For the ancient Persian sages, the difference is between fullness and deficiency, independence and need. These are two very different accounts. As long as existence is free from weakness and limitation, nothing other than existence can be joined to it—nothing that we could call an essence. Weakness and limitation belong to the lower levels of possible existence. Think of a shadow: it is not a separate, positive thing, but light diminished. These sages understand the lower levels of existence in the same way. Their limits arise from what makes each of them particular, without adding anything to the existence and light they share.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00426

Another objection: the Necessary Being is the source of possible beings. If He were pure existence, His being their source would either belong to existence itself or be something added to it. If it belonged to existence itself, then every existence would be a source of possible beings. That is impossible, since each possible being would then cause itself and its own causes. If instead the source were existence together with the condition of being separate from essence, the First Principle would be composite—and would not exist, since one of its supposed parts, separation from essence, is a mere absence. If the source were existence on the condition of being separate from essence, then any existence could be the source of every other existence; that relation would fail only when the condition of being a source—separation from essence—was absent.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00427

As before, there are two replies. Most of Aristotle’s followers ground this in God’s own particular existence, which differs in reality from all other existences. The ancient Persian sages ground it instead in the fullness and independence of His existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00428

Another objection: God's reality cannot be the same as the reality of anything else. Everything besides God entails possibility, while God's reality rules possibility out. Different necessary features require different underlying realities. Yet the Necessary Being's existence is like the existence of possible things in that both are existence. And since God is pure existence, there is nothing alongside that existence which is not His own reality. It follows, then, that every possible existence is equal to God's reality in its full nature.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00429

The reply is that the existence of possible things is not their essence, nor a part of it; it is something that belongs to their essence. But this answer is weak, because the fact that existence belongs to possible things does not prevent the Necessary Being from sharing with them the meaning of existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00430

Consider what follows from each kind of existence. Just as God’s reality differs from the essences of possible things in its necessary features, His existence differs from their existences in the features that follow from each. God’s existence is immaterial and necessary in itself; the existence of possible things is possible in itself and dependent on something else. If differences in necessary features prove a difference in the underlying realities, then God’s reality must differ in essence from the existences of possible things. That contradicts these philosophers’ position.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00431

Here is how Aristotle’s followers should answer. God’s existence and the existences of possible things are not the same in their own reality. They share only the general concept “existent,” which the mind forms when it thinks about things. Though that concept is one and the same, it follows from different realities. Sharing a concept does not make those realities identical.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00432

Another objection: if the Necessary Being is external existence itself—that is, existence in the absolute sense—then there must be several Necessary Beings, since the existence of a substance is not the existence of an accident. If instead He is existence on the condition that it is separate from essence, then He is composite, made up of existence and separation, which is a mere absence. That cannot be part of the Necessary Being. If He is existence with separation as a condition, then He is not necessary in Himself. But if He is something other than external existence, then either He exists without existence, which is impossible, or He exists with existence. In the latter case, existence must either be part of Him—which would make Him composite—or something outside Him, which is precisely the claim under dispute.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00433

Here is another way to make the point. We do not doubt that existence means being real. So the specific existence either includes this meaning of being and reality, or it does not. If it does not, it is not existence at all: a thing's specific existence is simply its being real. If it does include this meaning, then general existence belongs to it by its very nature. That general existence must either be a part of the Necessary Being or be the Necessary Being itself. Either way, He would have a universal essence, which is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00434

The answer to the first objection is that the Necessary Being is His own specific existence, wholly different from all other existences: He comes before them, rules over them, depends on nothing, and is their source. No one disputes that the general concept of existence, which is a mental notion like “thing,” can be added to this. But God's being existent in the sense of that through which something exists is nothing beyond His own reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00435

As the Shaykh states in The Book of Discussions, the Reality exists without an existence added to it from outside. It is not like humanity, which exists because it receives an existence beyond itself. The Reality is existence itself, with no additional existence laid over it. It is the reality of necessity itself—a simple meaning, even if we express it in several words.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00436

We can also apply the shared concept of existence to God. In that general sense, existence is a feature that necessarily belongs to Him and cannot be taken away, because He is real. But suppose someone says that God is existent in His own essence. We can then ask: does He have existence? If we allow that wording, we must mean the general concept of existence, which necessarily applies to Him. Or we can reject the wording: God is not a thing that possesses existence as an added feature. In his Annotations, the Shaykh chooses this second answer: when we say “the Necessary Being exists,” the wording is figurative and means “He is pure existence.” Later readers corrupted this into “His existence is necessary,” which is a mistake.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00437

For these philosophers, the Necessary Being’s own reality is a particular existence, while the shared concept of existence applies to it as well. One writer summarises their position this way: “The instance of existence found in the world is added to pure existence, the source of possible things, which is itself the reality of the Necessary Being.” This does not mean that God's existence is something added to His reality, or that He exists through two existences. There is no reason to treat one as a feature and the other as what bears it. No one disputes that the general concept of existence—and any particular application of that concept—is added to the distinct realities of the things it describes. The disagreement is only about whether God's own specific existence is identical to His reality or added to it. So if philosophers say that shared existence is identical with God but added to possible things, they mean that what makes the word “existent” truly apply to God is His own reality, without any other feature being joined to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00438

As for the other view, existence is not a universal, even though it is unbounded and shared. Think this through. If you understand how existence can be unbounded and shared without being a universal, you will be firmly grounded in knowledge.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00439

Another objection: everyone knows what existence means, while God's reality is unknown. What is known cannot be the same as what is unknown. The familiar answer is that what we know is existence in general, which differs from God's own specific reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00440
A flash of illumination
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00441

God's reality is not known to anyone through ideas or descriptions held in the mind; no philosopher or mystic would dispute this, and it has been proved. How could it be otherwise, when His reality is nothing but His own particular existence? A thing's particular existence cannot be multiplied, unlike an essence, which is an open-ended idea that can have many different forms of existence. Knowing something is simply one way that thing exists for an immaterial knower.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00442

But the claim that no one can know God's reality through full rational or sensory comprehension is also true. Our rational and sensory powers cannot master or encompass Him. Full mastery belongs to a cause in relation to its effect: the effect is one of the cause's expressions and is fully present to it, but the cause is never fully present to the effect.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00443

Yet it does not follow that no possible being can witness God at all. Each can turn toward His sacred reality, which lies beyond place, direction, and position, as far as something receiving a gift can attend to its giver. Each receives something of God’s self-disclosure according to its capacity for existence. What it cannot receive is limited by its own weakness and narrowness, and by its involvement with nonexistence, powers, and matter. The limit does not arise because God holds anything back. In His greatness, the breadth of His mercy, the intensity of His light, and its limitless reach, He is nearer to each of us than anyone else, as He says in the Qur'an: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.” And He says—“When My servants ask you about Me, I am near.” He is highest of all through the utmost perfection of His greatness, and nearest of all through the breadth of His mercy. He is exalted in His nearness and near in His exaltedness. A saying of the Prophet points to this: “If you were lowered into the deepest earth, you would come down upon God.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00444

Yaʿqub ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī says: “The First Cause is connected to us through what flows from it to us, while we are connected to it only through the Cause. So we may attend to it to the degree that a recipient can attend to its source. We should not measure how fully it encompasses us by how fully we can attend to it: its knowledge is richer, fuller, and more encompassing.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00445

The accomplished al-Shahrazūrī says in The Divine Tree: “The Necessary Being, necessary through Himself, is the most beautiful and perfect of all things. Every beauty and perfection is only a ray, a shadow, and an outpouring from His beauty and perfection. His majesty is supreme and His light overpowers all other light. He is veiled by the perfection of His radiance and the intensity of His appearing. The philosophers who know God and those who truly recognise Him witness Him, but they do not grasp Him in His full reality. The intensity of His appearing, the force of His radiance, and the weakness of our own immaterial, luminous selves keep us from that. The sun's brilliance and power prevent our eyes from grasping it, because its light is so intense. We know and witness the First Reality, but we do not encompass it with knowledge, as revelation says: ‘They do not encompass Him in knowledge,’ and, ‘All faces are humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting.’”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00446

When we say that an overwhelming light of the mind or the senses acts as a veil, we mean that our own powers fall short. They cannot fully grasp what they encounter. The veil lies in that shortcoming, not in the light itself. God’s reality is pure existence and pure light, untouched by nonexistence, darkness, weakness, or any flaw.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00447

Someone may ask: if spiritual souls can know God through direct presence, and what is witnessed through existence is His simple reality itself—not merely one aspect of it—how can that reality still be beyond our full understanding?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00448

We answer: no effect can witness God's reality except through a veil, or several veils. Even the first effect sees Him only through its own existence. In seeing itself, it witnesses the First Reality—but only as far as its own capacity allows, not in the fullness of the reality it witnesses.
